questions.question: For a compound Poisson process $S(t)$ recording cumulative claims from time 0, which formula records only claims arriving in $(a,b]$ for every realised path and every interval $0\le a<b$?

A compound Poisson loss process has stationary increments: $S(s+h)-S(s)$ has a law depending only on $h\ge0$. Which conclusion about different equal-length intervals is guaranteed for every such model?
options: Their realised loss increments must be equal.
Their loss increments have the same distribution.
Their cumulative endpoint totals have the same law.
Their loss paths must be constant in time.

questions.question: For $S(t)=\sum_{i=1}^{N(t)}X_i$, the count process is Poisson and the severity sequence is iid. Which additional relation is required for the usual compound Poisson process?
options: The severities are independent of the entire count process.
Every severity equals the waiting time before its claim.
Every severity is determined by its arrival time.
Every severity shares one random value across claims.

questions.question: A compound Poisson process has rate $\lambda>0$ and mean severity $\mu>0$. Its mean is $\lambda t\mu$, but a realised interval contains no arrivals. How does its loss path behave on that interval?
options: It increases continuously at rate $\lambda\mu$.
It resets to zero at the interval start.
It stays at its value at the interval start.
It grows by the mean severity at the interval end.

questions.question: A surplus path is $R(t)=u+ct-S(t)$, with initial capital $u$, premium income rate $c>0$ and cumulative claim process $S(t)$. A claim of amount $x>0$ arrives. Which jump-and-growth statement is valid for every such rate c and claim amount x?
options: It drops by c; between arrivals it grows at rate x.
It drops by x; between arrivals it grows at rate c.
It rises by x; between arrivals it grows at rate c.
It drops to u; between arrivals it remains constant.

questions.question: A compound Poisson process has claim rate 6 per year. What is the Poisson frequency parameter for cumulative claims during the first quarter of a year?
A compound Poisson process has claim rate 2 per year and independent iid severities with mean 50. What is expected cumulative loss at time $t=0.5$ years?
A compound Poisson process has rate 3 per year. Severity mean is 2 and variance is 1. What is the variance of cumulative loss over two years?
A compound Poisson process has rate 4 per year. Which count parameter governs its loss increment $S(3)-S(2.5)$, with times measured in years?
For surplus $R(t)=100+20t-S(t)$, time is in years. By time 2 there have been exactly two claims, of amounts 30 and 50. What is $R(2)$?

A compound Poisson process has rate $\lambda>0$ and strictly positive severities. For $0<s<t$, its disjoint increments are independent. Does that imply cumulative levels $S(s)$ and $S(t)$ are independent?
options: No; the later total includes the earlier claims.
Yes; every pair of process observations is independent.
Yes; stationary increments remove shared history.
No; the future increment must depend on the past.

questions.question: A compound Poisson process has strictly positive arrival rate and independent non-negative severities with positive probability of zero. Can the number of visible positive jumps always recover the arrival count $N(t)$?
options: Yes; every arrival must increase cumulative loss strictly.
Yes; Poisson arrivals cannot carry zero amounts.
No; each positive jump represents several simultaneous arrivals.
No; zero-amount arrivals leave no visible jump.

questions.question: A compound Poisson process has rate 12 per year. The same model is expressed in months, and a horizon is six months. Which rate and frequency parameter preserve its law?
options: Rate 12 per month; horizon parameter 72.
Rate 1 per month; horizon parameter 0.5.
Rate 1 per month; horizon parameter 6.
Rate 144 per month; horizon parameter 864.

questions.question: A compound Poisson process has rate 2 per year and strictly positive severities. What is the probability of zero loss in both disjoint intervals $(0,0.5]$ and $(1,2]$?
options: $\mathrm{e}^{-1}+\mathrm{e}^{-2}$.

questions.question: A compound Poisson process has rate3 per year and mean severity4. The event that its first-year total is100 has positive probability. What is the expected additional loss in the second year conditional on that first-year-total event?
A compound Poisson process has observed loss $S(1)=7$. Its rate is 2 per year and mean severity is 6. What is $\mathbb{E}[S(2)\mid S(1)=7]$, assuming this event has positive probability?

A Poisson arrival process has rate 1. Independently choose a common mark $Z$, equal to 0 or 2 with equal probabilities, and set $S(t)=ZN(t)$. Its expected loss is $t$. Does this mean curve guarantee independent loss increments?
options: No; separate increments share the unobserved mark.
Yes; independent arrival increments guarantee independent marked increments.
Yes; the expected loss is linear in elapsed time.
No; the arrival counts must themselves be dependent.

questions.question: A rate-1 Poisson process has arrival times $T_i$ and iid exponential gaps $G_i=T_i-T_{i-1}$, with $T_0=0$. Assign severity $X_i=G_i$ and define $S(t)=\sum_{i=1}^{N(t)}G_i$. Why is this not the usual compound Poisson construction despite iid non-negative marks?
options: The gaps cannot be identically distributed.
The gaps cannot be mutually independent.
The marks are tied to the arrival process itself.
The count cannot have a Poisson distribution at fixed time.

questions.question: A compound Poisson process has rate 2 and each independent severity is zero with probability $1/2$, otherwise positive. Over a unit-length interval the observed loss increment is zero. What is the conditional probability that the interval had no arrivals?
A surplus process is $R(t)=10+120t-100N(t)$ with rate-1 Poisson count $N(t)$ and time in years. Its expected drift is positive. Does that guarantee $R(0.1)\ge0$ almost surely?
options: Yes; positive expected drift gives a positive path slope everywhere.
Yes; the expected count 0.1 is less than one.
No; its expected drift is actually negative.
No; one early claim already makes capital negative.
